This rich chapter reveals vows and oaths as far more than legal instruments — they are gateways to the hidden divine light embedded in all of reality. The central teaching: through a vow (neder), a Jew exercises his unique power as a being of free choice to ascend to the level of Binah — the concealed Torah that preceded and underlies matan Torah — and from there to draw down a new obligatory light, transforming any neutral act into a complete mitzvah. An oath (shevuah) by contrast operates through Yesod, the revealed Torah's power of connection and sustenance. A dominant theme throughout is the power of the mouth and speech: the vow becomes real only when uttered aloud, for speech is the tzimtzum — the contraction that makes infinite light receivable. Conversely, violating one's word shatters the vessel of Chessed and allows the Sitra Achara to gain a grip. The Tzadik and the Sage stand at the center of this entire system: all vow-power derives from their attainment of the holy makifin; only they — or three Jews collectively embodying the three Patriarchs — possess the collective point (nekudah klalis) needed to dissolve and re-contract the light, thus annulling vows. Yom Kipur and Kol Nidrei are revealed as expressions of this very dynamic: the annual ascent to the level of Kodesh Kedoshim and Binah to release the spiritual constrictions of the year. The chapter also connects vows to oaths in legal disputes (entries 11–24), showing that every judicial oath is ultimately a moment of dvaikus — the litigant is drawn back to the primordial unity of truth where no falsehood can survive.

The central threads: The true Tzadik is the aspect of Moshe in every generation — composed of all the souls of Israel, standing between apostasy and divine Will. There is always one Tzadik who is the nekudas ha'emes [point of truth] among all the Tzadikim; the essential battle of the Sitra Achara in each generation is to conceal precisely this one. The essential cure is attachment — the hiskashrus — which is an unbreakable holy cord: one descends, and the Tzadik raises one by the cord from wherever one has fallen.

Death does not diminish the Tzadik — it magnifies him. After passing he ascends to where the living cannot go, and from there illuminates even more profoundly: gedolim tzadikim b'misasan yoser mi'bechayeihem. The grave becomes a holy site where all rectification is accessible. Weeping and seeking the Tzadik after his passing is itself a form of prayer and teshuvah.

The chapter contains a powerful social teaching: the holy gathering around the Tzadik multiplies houses of holiness through a combinatorial law — each soul added multiplies the houses exponentially, eventually encompassing even the most distant. The essential length of exile is the failure to seek the true Tzadik; and the cure is travel, searching, and self-sacrifice specifically to find and bind oneself to him — including his disciples and the books he left behind after his passing.
Otzar HaYirah — Treasury of Awe | Volume IV (נ–ת)

With 100 entries, this chapter is one of the richest in the collection. Its central teaching — drawn from dozens of Likutay Halachos — is that tzedakah is not merely a social act but a cosmic one: it is the human being's primary instrument for drawing divine abundance into the world, filling the moon's diminishment, and revealing the supernal will concealed behind nature.

The recurring tension is between chochmah tata'ah [lower wisdom / the Shechinah in exile] and chochmah ila'ah [upper wisdom / the source of Torah]. Money — rooted in the left / judgment — is the primary battleground of free choice. Tzedakah converts the left to the right; it is weighed against the entire Torah precisely because it accomplishes in the physical realm what the entire Torah accomplishes spiritually.

Gemilus chasadim — specifically the interest-free loan — is consistently placed above tzedakah. Its greater power lies in the waiting: by not pressing the borrower the lender nullifies the hold of time, which is the essential hold of the evil inclination. The prohibition of ribis [interest] is correspondingly severe — it strengthens time's grip and is considered tantamount to denying the entire Torah.

A recurring practical emphasis: tzedakah must be given to aniyim hagunim — worthy poor people, especially those attached to the true Tzadikim. Giving to unworthy poor — or to those who dispute the truth — does not rectify, and can actively increase the falsehood. One must pray greatly to Hashem to be led to worthy recipients.
Otzar HaYirah — Treasury of Awe | Volume IV (נ–ת)

This chapter of 32 entries weaves together a single grand teaching from many angles: the mitzvah of tzitzis is the primary instrument for rectifying the garments — the medameh [imaginative faculty] that clothes the intellect — so that the supernal light is received rather than blocked. The garments, left unrectified, become screens and obstacles; rectified through tzitzis, they become holy vessels for gradual, measured reception of infinite light.

Three interlocking themes recur throughout. First, the connection between tzitzis and the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy: the woolen threads are braided from the holy hairs — the hairsbreadth good points Hashem finds in every person — and from them the thread of Chessed is woven, sweetening all judgments. Second, tzitzis as the gathering of the dispersed — for their root is above place, and thereby they elevate everything trapped within place back to the Place of the world. Third, the precedence of tzitzis over tefilin: faith must precede intellect — one cannot receive the totality of mochin without first wrapping in the light of Atika D'Atikin from which faith flows.

Notable is the practical emphasis: tzitzis protect against licentiousness (the fringes literally redirect the eyes), against harmful forces, against forgetting the divine purpose. The tekheles thread directs the gaze toward the tachlis — and the child's very first mitzvah is tzitzis, for this gaze must be established before all else.
Otzar HaYirah — Treasury of Awe | Volume IV (נ–ת)

Though the shortest chapter in the volume at ten entries, this chapter touches the deepest ground. Its opening establishes the spatial logic of holiness: the more physical a place, the more constrained and distant from the divine; the more holy, the closer to the Place of the world — where space itself dissolves. This maps kedushah onto the entire project of Torah: drawing the infinite into the finite.

Entry 5 presents the ten of the minyan as a kabbalistic necessity — not a social threshold but a cosmic structure: the ten sefiros from Keter to Malchus are all required to join the attainment of the upper realms (ayeh makom kevodo — where is He?) with the lower realms (melo kol ha'aretz kevodo — He fills everything). Only when all ten are present can these two poles of awareness be united in a single act of communal sanctification.

Entry 7 is the most extensive — a profound meditation on the paradox of mesirat nefesh. The Torah was given for life, and ordinarily one transgresses rather than dies. But when the Sitra Achara grows strong enough to feed from holy mercy itself — it seeks to swallow souls. Then the body of the martyr becomes the instrument of cosmic reversal: standing in the Sitra Achara's gullet, it forces the disgorging of all swallowed holiness. This is the secret of the ten martyrs and of all Jewish martyrdom throughout history.
Entry 8 is a single line of crystalline teaching: the essential holiness is humility and lowliness.
Otzar HaYirah — Treasury of Awe | Volume IV (נ–ת)

This compact three-entry chapter draws a striking connection between the physical difficulty of birth and the spiritual battle that surrounds every new soul entering the world. Each Jewish soul brings a new revelation of G-d's presence — and the husk of Amalek, whose essence is denial and doubt, specifically attempts to obstruct that birth. Prayer and faith are the antidotes, and Psalm 100 in particular — with its declaration that Hashem is G-d and its evocation of faith flowing through the generations — is the traditional segulah for easing labor.

Entry 3 extends this teaching to medicine generally: healing and suffering both flow from the same divine source — the Yad HaChazakah — and therefore true healing often requires passing through bitterness first.
Otzar HaYirah — Treasury of Awe | Volume IV (נ–ת)

With 44 entries, this is one of the richest chapters in the volume and one of the most personally applicable. Its central thesis: the ratzon — the will — is the indestructible core of the Jewish soul. It is drawn from the will of all wills, rooted above where no sin reaches, and it is therefore the one thing no external force can truly destroy. Even after every fall, the will can be renewed — and this renewal is itself the beginning of all redemption.

Entry 28 is perhaps the most practically important: there is no despair whatsoever. Even from the very lowest depths — even one who has sinned greatly and repeatedly — as long as the will is alive and one keeps saying "I want to return to Hashem," there is hope. The will itself, apart from any action, is already precious before Hashem.

Entry 11 teaches the secret of holy stubbornness: since external obstacles can always overpower external actions, the only unconquerable force is the inner will. One can always be prevented from traveling, from learning, from praying as one wishes. But no force in the world can prevent one from wanting. And Hashem glories specifically in this indomitable inner will of Israel.

The chapter closes with a practical instruction (entry 44): even the words one speaks about one's desires matter — for words of good longing create good souls in the world that go on to arouse others toward good.
Otzar HaYirah — Treasury of Awe | Volume IV (נ–ת)

This single-entry chapter is a sharp warning: compassion itself — the most essential human attribute — can be hijacked by the Sitra Achara. The pattern is ancient: those who caused the Golden Calf did so in the name of the people's welfare. And the same pattern repeats throughout history when movements that claim to act out of care for the Jewish people lead them away from Torah.

The Hebrew verse chosen for the chapter's opening — rachmei resha'im achzari, "the mercies of the wicked are cruel" — captures this precisely: the cruelest acts are often wrapped in the language of compassion. The antidote is the true Tzadik — who knows the difference between genuine mercy rooted in holiness and the pseudo-mercy that serves the Sitra Achara.
Otzar HaYirah — Treasury of Awe | Volume IV (נ–ת)

The longest chapter since Tzadik, at 68 entries. The chapter's thesis is that peace is not merely a social virtue — it is the cosmic mechanism through which separated fragments of the divine light can be received without shattering. Every soul of Israel is a vessel — and the light of G-dliness requires all vessels assembled together in love and peace to be received safely. This is why the Torah required 600,000 present at Sinai, and why love of one's neighbor is declared the great principle of the Torah.

A recurring and powerful idea is the interplay between truth and peace (entry 20): Hashem cast truth to the ground not because truth is unimportant, but because a truth that fuels accusation and dispute is not the truth He desires. The Torah-scholar knows to set aside divisive truth for peace's sake — and paradoxically, this specific yielding is itself the truest path to bringing genuine truth into the world.

Entry 52 distinguishes partial peace from general peace: not harming one's fellow is partial; giving of one's own to another, yielding beyond obligation — that is the general peace. And the same principle applies inward: not sinning is partial inner peace; fully subordinating all bodily desires to the soul is the complete inner peace.
